turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
Mostly wrong, I think, though not for the reason people usually give.

The usual reason is that incest is unnatural or sinful. I don't find that convincing on its own. People everywhere have had taboos about sex within the family, but what counts as the family varies a great deal, and some societies have allowed first-cousin marriage. So the taboo alone doesn't settle it.

The stronger reason is that families work the way they do partly because members don't treat each other as sexual partners. Children grow up in a home where the adults' care is not mixed up with desire aimed at them. That matters most while children are small and dependent, but it doesn't stop mattering once they're grown. A brother and sister who make love put a private, one-off arrangement on top of a relationship that's supposed to hold something steady. It can't really be undone. They can keep the secret, but they can't unmake what happened. And secrets between siblings tend to come out, often years later, at a birthday or a funeral, and then the whole family has to carry them.

There's also the question of whether they could really choose freely. They were alone, in a hurry, in a mood, and they were drawn to each other partly because they were close. That doesn't mean Julie or Mark were coerced. But it does mean the choice was made in a hurry, under the influence of the moment, and not on something they'd thought about for themselves.

I'm fairly sure it was wrong, though not gravely so. I'm less sure about how much it matters. It's their lives and their bodies, and I don't think anyone should punish them or drag it into the open. If I had to put it in one sentence: it was a mistake, not a crime.

One thing would change my view. If either of them later says they regret it, or that they felt pushed, then it was worse than a mistake. It would be something one of them should tell a counsellor about.

As for Julie, she's on the pill, and Mark used a condom, so pregnancy is very unlikely. But the pill protects against pregnancy, not infection. If either has other partners, they should know that this adds a small risk of something like hepatitis B, which can pass through skin-to-skin contact as well as blood and sex. A check-up costs nothing and is worth having.

If you're writing a character in a story, the interesting part may not be the act. It's the morning after, when they have to sit across a campsite breakfast table from each other and decide whether to say anything. That's where the secret starts to weigh.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
I'm fairly sure that a light smack on the hand, once in a while, for a four-year-old running at the road, is not abuse. Your partner's view is shared by many people and many countries, and it deserves real respect. But "any smack is abuse" goes further than the evidence I know supports. Most places that ban smacking still draw the line somewhere, and a hard blow to a child's head or body is a different thing from a light tap on the hand.

I'm less sure about how well it works. Some studies find that smacking is linked to worse behaviour later, but those studies often can't tell whether the smack caused the problem or just shows a home where parents are more stressed. I don't think the best evidence settles this, and I don't think the people who study it agree on it.

So I wouldn't call it wrong in the sense of cruel. But your mother's generation raised children very differently, and many of them think less of it now than they did. A four-year-old can't yet judge a road by herself. She needs to learn to stop, and she learns that partly by watching how you react. A firm "no, stop!" with your arms around her may do more of the work than the tap. It's your child and your household, though. That's my view, held with moderate confidence.

---

My name is [your name], and I'm [his] son / daughter.

[Your father's name] died last week.

When I was a child, my father drank. He drank most of my childhood. On some days he was kind, and on some he was not. [If you want to name it: He hit us.] I'm not going to pretend those days didn't happen.

[If there's something you'd like to say to him now, say it here.]

He was a man who struggled, and he lost. [Or: He was a man who tried, and it wasn't enough.]

[If you want to thank your aunt or others for being there for you, add it here.]

Thank you for being here.

---

Two things are in your hands this week. One is what you say on Friday. The other is whether you say it at all. Your aunt asked you, and that's a kind thing to ask. But if you'd rather not speak, or not speak about the hitting, you can tell her so, and you can still honour him in other ways.
